title: Acute asthma: recognising severity and first actions
blurb: Grade an adult asthma attack using SIGN 158 and start the right first treatments: oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and steroids.
question: Mr Oduya, 24, arrives in ED with asthma. He can only say a few words per breath, his respiratory rate is 28/min, pulse 116/min, PEF 40% of his best and SpO2 94% on air. How severe is this attack, and what are the first treatments?

teach.body: Formally: the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline (NG245) does not cover acute attacks; BTS and SIGN retained the SIGN 158 recommendations for managing acute asthma in adults. In plain English: grade the attack using PEF, breathing, pulse, speech and SpO2, then treat fast with oxygen, high-dose inhaled bronchodilators and early steroids. Deaths from asthma are often linked to failure to recognise severity, so measure, do not guess.

bands.label: PEF 33–50%, RR 25+, HR 110+, can't finish sentences
PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, silent chest, exhaustion

teach.caption: Any ONE feature places the patient in the more severe band. Use the person's best PEF; use predicted only if a recent best (within two years) is unknown.

head: Clinical signs
Measurements
teach.caption: A 'normal' PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a danger sign: they are tiring. A raised PaCO2 means near-fatal asthma.

steps.label: Ipratropium 0.5 mg
steps.sub: if severe, life-threatening or poor response

teach.caption: Repeat β2 agonist every 15–30 minutes, or give continuous nebulisation (5–10 mg/hour), if the response is inadequate.

teach.body: In acute severe or life-threatening asthma, nebulisers are driven by oxygen (at least 6 L/min) because air-driven nebulisers can cause desaturation. Mild to moderate attacks can be treated with repeated puffs of a pMDI through a large-volume spacer. Do not delay oxygen if an oximeter is not yet available. This is the reverse of hypercapnic COPD, where nebulisers are driven by air.

rows.label: IV magnesium sulphate
values: Single dose, acute severe, poor response, senior advice

rows.label: Sedation
values: Unless for anaesthetic or ICU procedures

rows.label: PEF before and after each β2 dose
Repeat gas within 1 hour if PaCO2 normal or raised

teach.note: ICU referral if failing to respond: deteriorating PEF, persisting or worsening hypoxia, hypercapnia, falling pH, exhaustion, drowsiness or respiratory arrest.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Oduya in ED
teach.body: Mr Oduya cannot complete sentences, his respiratory rate is 28, pulse 116 and PEF 40% of best: acute severe asthma (any one feature is enough). His SpO2 is 94%, so no life-threatening feature yet. Nurse Bea gives oxygen to keep 94–98%, an oxygen-driven salbutamol 5 mg nebuliser and prednisolone 40–50 mg, adds ipratropium 0.5 mg as he is acute severe, and records PEF 15–30 minutes later. He stays under senior review in case he needs IV magnesium.

teach.text: SpO2 cut-off confusion: in acute asthma, SpO2 BELOW 92% is a life-threatening feature, but the oxygen TARGET is 94–98%. They are different numbers for different jobs. And a quiet, 'calm' patient may have a silent chest and exhaustion, not improvement.

items.label: PEF 1 hour after treatment: may go home

items: Grade with SIGN 158: any one feature puts the patient in the higher band.
Life-threatening: PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, silent chest, exhaustion, 'normal' PaCO2.
Oxygen to 94–98%; high-dose salbutamol, oxygen-driven if severe; repeat every 15–30 minutes.
Prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for at least 5 days; ipratropium if severe; IV magnesium after senior advice.
Before discharge: PEF above 75%, technique checked, action plan, GP follow-up within 2 working days.

summary: You can now grade an adult asthma attack as moderate, acute severe, life-threatening or near-fatal using SIGN 158, and start oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and steroids correctly. You also know when to escalate to IV magnesium or ICU and what is needed before discharge.

A.q: An adult with an asthma attack has a PEF of 45% of best, a respiratory rate of 22 and can speak in full sentences. How is this attack classified?
A.why: SIGN 158 Table 15: any one of PEF 33–50%, RR 25 or more, HR 110 or more, or inability to complete sentences makes it acute severe. PEF 45% is enough.

whyNot.0: Moderate asthma has PEF above 50–75% and no acute severe features.
whyNot.2: Life-threatening needs a feature such as PEF below 33% or SpO2 below 92%.
whyNot.3: Near-fatal means raised PaCO2 or needing mechanical ventilation.

A.q: Which finding indicates life-threatening asthma in an adult?
A.why: SIGN 158: SpO2 below 92% is a life-threatening feature.

whyNot.0: HR 110 or more is an acute severe feature.
whyNot.1: RR 25 or more is an acute severe feature.
whyNot.2: PEF 33–50% is an acute severe feature.

A.q: What oral prednisolone dose does SIGN 158 recommend for an adult with an acute asthma attack?
A.why: SIGN 158 9.3.3: prednisolone 40–50 mg daily, continued until recovery (minimum 5 days).

whyNot.0: 30 mg for 5 days is the COPD exacerbation regimen.
whyNot.2: 20 mg for 3 days is too low and too short.
whyNot.3: Higher doses are not more effective, and the course is not 10 days fixed.

B.q: A woman with acute severe asthma needs a salbutamol nebuliser. How should it be driven?
options: By oxygen at 6 L/min or more
By an air compressor at home rate
B.why: SIGN 158: oxygen-driven nebulisers are preferred in acute severe or life-threatening asthma because of the risk of desaturation with air; most nebulisers need about 6 L/min.

whyNot.1: Air-driven nebulisers risk desaturation in acute asthma.
whyNot.2: 2 L/min is too low to drive most nebulisers.
whyNot.3: Air compressors are used for hypercapnic COPD, not acute asthma.

B.q: A man with acute severe asthma responds poorly to initial salbutamol. Which drug should be added to the nebuliser?
B.why: SIGN 158 9.3.4: add nebulised ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg 4–6 hourly for acute severe or life-threatening asthma or a poor initial response.

whyNot.0: Nebulised magnesium is not recommended in adults.
whyNot.1: Nebulised adrenaline has no significant benefit over salbutamol.
whyNot.3: Nebulised steroid is not the recommended add-on; systemic steroids are given.

B.q: When should PEF be measured after starting treatment for acute asthma?
B.why: SIGN 158 9.4: measure and record PEF 15–30 minutes after starting treatment, then according to response, and before and after each β2 agonist.

whyNot.0: 60 minutes is too late for the first reassessment.
whyNot.2: PEF guides treatment throughout, not only at discharge.

C.q: Ms Quinn, 31, with acute severe asthma, has had salbutamol, ipratropium and prednisolone. Her PEF has stayed at 38% and she is tiring. A blood gas shows PaCO2 5.2 kPa. What is the priority?
options: Reassure her that the gas is normal
Switch her nebuliser to an air drive
Repeat PEF at the next observations
C.why: A 'normal' PaCO2 in acute severe asthma is a life-threatening feature, and exhaustion with a persistently low PEF signals failure to respond: urgent senior review, consider IV magnesium and ICU (SIGN 158).

whyNot.0: A normal PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic indicates tiring, not safety.
whyNot.2: Oxygen-driven nebulisers are preferred in severe asthma.

C.q: A doctor prescribes IV magnesium for a man with acute severe asthma and a poor response to inhaled therapy. Which regimen fits SIGN 158?
options: 2 g IV over 2 minutes, repeated hourly
5 g IV over 4 hours as an infusion
C.why: SIGN 158 9.3.5: a single dose of IV magnesium sulphate 1.2–2 g over 20 minutes for acute severe asthma with a poor initial response, after senior consultation.

whyNot.1: Rapid repeated doses risk hypermagnesaemia; repeat dosing has not been assessed.
whyNot.2: This dose and duration are not the SIGN 158 regimen.
whyNot.3: Nebulised magnesium is not recommended in adults.

C.q: Mr Lee, 40, admitted with acute asthma, is now improving. Which finding supports safe discharge under SIGN 158?
options: PEF 60% of best with mild wheeze
C.why: SIGN 158 discharge criteria: on discharge medication for 12–24 hours, inhaler technique checked and recorded, PEF above 75% of best or predicted and diurnal variability below 25%, with steroids, an action plan and follow-up.

whyNot.0: PEF 60% is below the discharge threshold.
whyNot.1: Patients should be on discharge medication for 12–24 hours.
whyNot.3: SpO2 92% is borderline and does not meet the target of 94–98%.

reteach.title: Count the features, take the worst
reteach.question: If a patient has a mix of moderate and severe features, which band do you choose?

blocks.body: Asthma severity is graded by the single worst feature. A man speaking in full sentences with a PEF of 30% has life-threatening asthma, because PEF below 33% is a life-threatening feature. A woman with a normal PEF but a pulse of 115 and a respiratory rate of 27 has acute severe asthma. Grade on the worst, treat on the worst, and regrade after every treatment.

root.label: Any life-threatening feature?
root.sub: PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, silent chest, exhaustion

blocks.text: Raised PaCO2 is near-fatal asthma, not 'just' life-threatening: it needs immediate anaesthetic and critical care help.

explain.body: Any one of: PEF 33–50% of best or predicted, respiratory rate 25/min or more, heart rate 110/min or more, or inability to complete sentences in one breath.

test.q: Which heart rate is an acute severe asthma feature in an adult under SIGN 158?
test.why: SIGN 158 Table 15: heart rate 110/min or more is an acute severe feature.

whyNot.3: 130/min exceeds it, but the threshold is 110.

explain.body: Any one in severe asthma: altered consciousness, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, cyanosis, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, PEF below 33%, SpO2 below 92%, PaO2 below 8 kPa, 'normal' PaCO2.

test.q: During an asthma attack a previously wheezy patient becomes quiet with almost no breath sounds. What does this suggest?
options: A good response to the salbutamol
test.why: A silent chest is a life-threatening feature: so little air is moving that wheeze cannot be heard.

whyNot.0: Improvement brings better air entry, not silence.
whyNot.2: Loss of breath sounds is not a sign of resolution.
whyNot.3: Anxiety does not remove breath sounds.

explain.body: Oxygen to 94–98%; salbutamol 5 mg by oxygen-driven nebuliser in severe attacks, repeated every 15–30 minutes if needed; prednisolone 40–50 mg (or hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly IV); ipratropium 0.5 mg if severe.

test.q: An adult with acute asthma cannot swallow tablets. Which steroid fits SIGN 158?
test.why: SIGN 158 9.3.3: parenteral hydrocortisone 400 mg daily (100 mg six-hourly) is as effective as higher doses when tablets cannot be taken.

whyNot.1: Inhaled steroid does not replace systemic steroids in an attack.
whyNot.2: Dexamethasone 16 mg is not the SIGN 158 regimen.
whyNot.3: 5 mg is far below the 40–50 mg dose.

explain.body: On discharge medicines for 12–24 hours, inhaler technique checked, PEF above 75% with diurnal variability below 25%, steroids and inhaled steroid, own PEF meter and action plan, GP follow-up within 2 working days.

test.q: After discharge from hospital for acute asthma, when should GP follow-up be arranged?
test.why: SIGN 158 discharge criteria: GP follow-up arranged within 2 working days (and respiratory clinic within 4 weeks).

whyNot.1: 2 weeks is too late given the risk of death in the month after discharge.
whyNot.2: 4 weeks is the respiratory clinic timeframe, not GP.
whyNot.3: The annual review is far too late.
